title: Influence of Heat Input Variation on the Metallurgical Features of the Heat-Affected Zone in API 5L X65 Welded Joints
content: Understanding the influence of heat input on the microstructural evolution of welded pipeline steels is essential for ensuring mechanical integrity and operational reliability. In this study, the effects of different heat inputs on the microstructural transformations in buttered joints of API 5L X65 PSL2 steel welded by robotic Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) were evaluated. The process was carried out using a shielding gas mixture of 85% Ar and 15% CO₂ with pulsed metal transfer, employing three heat input levels, 0.8, 0.9, and 1.0 kJ.mm⁻¹, classified as low, medium, and high, respectively. A buttering layer was deposited on one side of a half-V groove to generate a linear thermal-affected region using the same welding parameters. Microstructural characterization was performed through optical and scanning electron microscopy, complemented by X-ray diffraction to detect brittle phases formed during thermal cycling. Vickers microhardness measurements HV(0.1) were conducted across three regions of the welds. Results indicated that higher heat input produced a wider thermally altered region. Martensite was detected in the coarse-grained area under all conditions, contributing to increased hardness values. In contrast, regions subjected to intercritical and subcritical cycles exhibited lower hardness due to tempering effects and reduced phase transformation.
